objects.docstring: The poetry namespace.

poetry-agent: the agent-interop gem of the poetry family - the
surfaces through which agents reach the component contract, built
once (the registry) and projected many ways:

- {MCP::Server} - the boot-free `poetry-agent` MCP server, on the
  official `mcp` gem (discover:
  list_components / describe_component / check / compose / build_page
  / get_skill) for coding agents in editors.
- {WebMCP} - the in-page runtime: rendered components' declared tools
  (`tool` declarations in poetry-core) registered with the browser's
  `document.modelContext` for the user's own agent (operate), plus the
  declarative-form path and the origin-trial delivery.
- {A2UI} - the registry projected as an A2UI catalog (the vocabulary
  an agent generates declarative UI against).
- {AGUI} - the Rails-side AG-UI client: an agent backend's event stream
  folded into chat frames and relayed as versioned Turbo Streams,
  with the component tools the browser executes advertised as the
  agent's frontend tools.

Both read the same committed registries; neither is a second source.

objects.docstring:
The A2UI surface: Google's declarative generative-UI format, where
an agent emits a flat component list against a client-owned catalog
and the client renders it with its own components. Two halves ship:

- {Catalog} projects Poetry's registry into an A2UI v1.0 catalog
  document, so any A2UI agent generates against Poetry's vocabulary
  and a renderer validates what arrives against the same document.
- The renderer: {Session} folds the envelope (`createSurface`,
  `updateComponents`, `updateDataModel`, `deleteSurface`) into
  {Surface}s, {Renderer} renders a surface through the host's view
  context with a catalog binding ({Catalogs::Basic} for the spec's
  basic catalog, {Catalogs::Native} for Poetry's own), {Streams}
  delivers changes as versioned Turbo Streams, and a submitted
  surface form becomes the spec's `action` message
  ({Session#action}). {Functions} holds the basic catalog's function
  set - the `formatString` grammar ({Expression}), the formatters,
  the validators behind `checks` ({Checks}) - which {Evaluator} runs
  for both catalogs.

objects.docstring:
The `formatString` grammar: literal text with `${...}` blocks, each
block a data path, a literal, or a function call whose arguments are
named (`name: expression`, comma separated, a trailing comma allowed)
and are expressions again; `\${` is a literal `${`. Parsing yields a
plain tree the {Evaluator} walks:

  [:template, nodes]           the whole string
  [:text, "literal text"]
  [:path, "/absolute"]         or a relative path (`name`, `./name`, `../name`)
  [:literal, 12] / [:literal, "quoted"] / [:literal, true]
  [:call, "formatDate", { "value" => node, "format" => node }]

The spec's rules: a path is a run of identifier characters, `/`, `.`
and `-` (Poetry adds `~`, so a JSON Pointer's escapes read); a
number takes an optional sign, a mantissa (`5`, `5.`, `5.25`, `.5`)
and an optional exponent, and is an error outside the double range
and zero below it; a string unescapes `\n`, `\t` and `\r` and keeps
any other escaped character; `null` reads as the empty string;
nesting stops at {MAX_DEPTH}.

objects.docstring:
JSON Schema 2020-12 validation for the subset the A2UI specification's
message schemas, common types and catalogs use, with nothing beyond
the standard library. It is the strict tier's schema half: the
message envelope, each component against its catalog entry, each
function call against its catalog function.

Documents are given by URI ({.compile} indexes them); a root and
everything it reaches compile once, at construction, so a schema the
interpreter cannot honour raises there ({Unsupported}, {UnknownRef})
and never halfway through a message. Validation only reads the
compiled nodes, so one {Schema} serves every instance, from any
thread. Several roots over the same documents share one {Compiler}
({.compile}, then {Compiler#schema}).

A node evaluates an instance in one pass and answers with the
property names it evaluated, which flow through `$ref`, `allOf`, the
passing `anyOf`/`oneOf` branches and `if`/`then`/`else` to the
`unevaluatedProperties` that closes an object. {#valid?} stops at
the first failing keyword; {#errors} walks on, and explains a failed
`oneOf` or `anyOf` through the branch the instance most likely meant.

Two shortcuts keep the walk linear on A2UI's nested function calls:
a `oneOf` whose branches all require one property with distinct
string constants evaluates only the branch the instance names (the
catalog unions, `FunctionCall`), and a branch whose `type` excludes
the instance's JSON type is skipped as failed. Detection falls back
to evaluating every branch whenever it cannot prove the shortcut.

Unknown keywords are annotations, as 2020-12 requires; a 2020-12
keyword the interpreter does not implement, another draft, an
embedded `$id` resource or a pattern whose meaning would differ from
ECMA-262 is refused at compile time. A walk nested deeper than
{MAX_DEPTH} raises {LimitError} instead of exhausting the stack.

uri = "https://a2ui.org/specification/v1_0/agent_to_renderer.json"
schema = Poetry::Agent::A2UI::Schema.new(documents: { uri => doc, ... }, root: uri)
schema.valid?(message) # => true or false
schema.errors(message) # => [] or [Schema::Problem, ...]

compiler = Poetry::Agent::A2UI::Schema.compile(documents) # several roots, one compilation
component = compiler.schema("#{uri}#/$defs/Component")

The schema half of strict validation: the A2UI specification's own
schemas (each protocol version's message schema, its common types and
its basic catalog, shipped unmodified under `schemas/` with their
Apache-2.0 LICENSE) with a surface's catalogs plugged in where the
message schema says `catalog.json`.

A catalog plugs in as the specification's own test runner plugs one:
its `$id` moves beside the common types so its relative references
resolve, a `#/$defs/X` it does not define points at the common types,
and the `anyComponent` and `anyFunction` unions are built from its
`components` and `functions` when it states none. A catalog entry
closed with `additionalProperties: false` is opened to the envelope
keys (`id`, `component`, `catalogId`, ...), which the SDKs strip before
they apply an entry. On v1.0, where a component or call may name its
own catalog, `catalog.json` dispatches on `catalogId`: none is the
surface's default, a held catalog is that catalog, and one the
session does not hold passes here and is refused as a catalog error.

The renderer-side consumer of the A2UI envelope: applies
`createSurface`, `updateComponents`, `updateDataModel`, and
`deleteSurface` to a set of {Surface}s, answers what it cannot
honor with renderer-to-agent error messages, and turns a
submitted form into the spec's `action` message.

Each surface speaks the protocol version of the message that created
it, v0.9 and v1.0 side by side ({Dialect}): a later message must
speak the same one, and whatever the session sends about a surface
carries its version (`"v0.9"`, or v1.0's `"1.0"`). Every message
names its version; v1.0's earlier spelling `"v1.0"` is accepted.

  component, and every component is reachable from the root;
- identifiers: a v1.0 component id and function name is a UAX #31
  identifier, and every call names a function its catalog declares;

objects.docstring:
One A2UI surface on the renderer side: its flat component list
(an adjacency list keyed by id, `root` at the top), its data
model, and a monotonic version the Turbo Stream delivery compares.
A surface belongs to a catalog binding, which knows how each
component references its children; the surface itself is
catalog-agnostic beyond that. In v1.0 a component or a function call
may name its own catalog (`catalogId`) among the surface's catalogs
(the session's, of the surface's version); one that names none uses
the surface's default, which a v1.0 surface may not have. There is no
fallback: an unknown catalog is an error. A surface speaks the
protocol version that created it ({Dialect}): v1.0's `{ "@path" }`
bindings, or v0.9's `{ "path" }`.

objects.docstring:
The AG-UI surface: a Rails-side CLIENT of the Agent-User Interaction
protocol. An agent backend (any AG-UI integration, or a Ruby server)
streams events - text deltas, tool calls, state, activities, run
lifecycle, interrupts - and this module turns that stream into
server-rendered chat frames a Hotwire page updates through Turbo
Streams, the same pipeline the chat replay rig proves.

The pieces, each usable alone:

- {SSE} parses `text/event-stream` chunks into event hashes.
- {Client} POSTs a run to an AG-UI endpoint and yields its events.
- {RunInput} builds the `RunAgentInput` wire hash, and
  {.tool_descriptor} advertises a rendered component's declared
  tools as frontend-defined tools the browser executes.
- {Transcript} folds events into messages (Chat-shaped parts),
  shared state (JSON Patch), activities, the run status, pending
  client tools, and interrupts.
- {Relay} renders each change as a versioned Turbo Stream through a
  host-supplied row renderer, plus the client-tool bridge element
  the `poetry--agent--agui-client-tool` controller executes.

Nothing here calls a model: the agent is whatever the host points
the client at.

AG-UI 1.0 enforcement: unrecognised material is dropped or stripped
with a warning, a malformed known value is fatal. Driven only by the
contract table (config/agui/contract-1.0.json, generated from the
vendored 1.0 schema by `rake agui:contract`), one pass per event. It
mirrors the reference client's strip stage (what is stripped, where,
and the reported paths) and the validation that follows it (what is
fatal). Adapted from an MIT-licensed source (THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

The input is never mutated; a value comes back as the same object when
nothing inside it changed (copy on write).

op, a missing path, a failed test).

The AG-UI 1.0 processing pipeline, in the order the specification
fixes:

  compatibility boundary -> middleware -> enforcement -> chunk expansion -> verification -> application

One instance per stream; {Client#run} and {Relay} each hold one.
Everything it returns is verified, expanded and camelCase, so the
{Transcript} is a plain reducer of it. In strict mode (the conformant
default) a rejection raises {ProtocolError}; the opt-in lenient mode,
for developing against an agent that is not yet conformant, drops the
offending event with a warning instead, and reads snake_case keys.

row renderer (its own partial or component: a message and its
version in, the row's HTML out - the row must carry

objects.docstring:
Folds an AG-UI event stream into what a chat page renders: the
messages in order, each as Chat-shaped parts
(`{kind: :text, text:, state:}`, `{kind: :reasoning, text:, state:}`,
`{kind: :tool, name:, input:, output:, state:, tool_call_id:, metadata:}`,
`{kind: :media, part:}` for a non-text content part), the shared
state (snapshots and JSON Patch deltas), activities, every run's
status, outcome and interrupts, the subagent invocations, and the
tool calls the browser must execute before the next run. A text or
reasoning part is `state: :streaming` until its END event (or the
run's end) closes it, then `:done` - the difference between
"Thinking" and "Thought". A reasoning message is a message of its
own (role `reasoning`), as in AG-UI 1.0.

A tool result is a message of its own too, as the protocol models
it, kept in the conversation but not among the {#messages} a page
renders: its call's part reads the answer (`output`, `state`). So
a result that arrives before its call, one whose call never comes,
and a second result for one call all survive, and
{#messages_for_input} sends each result right after the call it
answers, as providers require.

Metadata merges into what each event builds, key by key, the last
write winning: a message, a tool call, a tool result, an activity.
A message carries the `subagentRunId` of the invocation that built
it. An encrypted reasoning value is held apart from the parts and
returned only in {#messages_for_input}, to the producer that issued
it.

It reduces VERIFIED events: what a {Pipeline} delivers (Client#run and
Relay route the wire through one), so every chunk is already expanded,
every id present, and every open item closed by the stream itself. A
patch it cannot apply, an activity delta with nothing to patch, an
encrypted value naming nothing it holds, or text aimed at an activity
message is a {ProtocolWarning}.

Every change bumps {#version}, and {#apply} answers the ids of the
messages it touched, so a relay re-renders exactly those rows with
a monotonic version the page's versioned replace honors.

objects.docstring:
Stream verification, a port of the TypeScript client's verify/verify.ts:
the run lifecycle, open/close discipline for every streamed entity,
ownership agreement on `subagentRunId`, and nothing open at RUN_FINISHED.
It runs after enforcement and chunk expansion, so it sees schema-valid,
expanded events only.

  verify = Verification.new
  verify.call(event) # => event, or raises ProtocolError (stage :verification)

Every check runs before any state changes, so a rejected event leaves the
tracking exactly as it was (lenient mode drops it and carries on).

Not ported, because enforcement already rejects the same events: the
`subagentRunId: null` tolerance, the lifecycle-optional null checks, the
SUBAGENT_* "without a 'subagentRunId' / 'name' / 'message'" checks, the
outcome-type and interruptIds checks, and the nested-null checks on
snapshot messages and interrupts. verify.ts keeps them for in-process
producers that skip enforcement; this pipeline has no such path.

objects.docstring:
MCP Apps, the author's side: a Rails app's own MCP server (on the
official `mcp` gem) serves Poetry-rendered screens as the interactive
UI a host such as Claude shows inside its chat. A {Document} is one
`ui://` resource, a complete HTML page rendered through the app's own
views and layout-free of the host page: Poetry's stylesheet and
controllers reach it from the app's origin (or inlined), and the
bridge (`@poetry/agent/mcp_app`) speaks the spec's JSON-RPC over
postMessage to the host. A tool answers with a {Result}: text for the
model, data in `structuredContent`, and {Fragment}s of server-rendered
HTML in `_meta`, which the bridge applies by region the way Turbo
Streams apply, so the page stays a template and the data stays with
the call.

The server, the transport, consent, the sandbox and the iframe are the
gem's and the host's; what Poetry adds is the document, the fragments
and the bridge.

examples.text:
PLANS = Poetry::Agent::Apps::Document.new(uri: "ui://shop/plans", name: "plans",
                                          template: "apps/plans", origin: "https://shop.example")
server = MCP::Server.new(name: "shop", capabilities: Poetry::Agent::Apps.capabilities,
                         resources: [PLANS.resource])
server.resources_read_handler(&Poetry::Agent::Apps.reader(PLANS))
server.define_tool(name: "show_plans", meta: PLANS.tool_meta) do |team_size: nil|
  Poetry::Agent::Apps.result(text: "Three plans; Pro fits #{team_size}.",
                             data: { "recommended" => "pro" },
                             fragments: [Poetry::Agent::Apps.fragment("plans", partial: "apps/plans/table",
                                                                      locals: { team_size: team_size })])
end

objects.docstring:
One `ui://` resource: the complete HTML document a host loads into
its sandbox, rendered through the app's own views, and the metadata
(`_meta.ui`) the host reads beside it.

Assets reach the sandbox two ways. `assets: :absolute` (the default)
links the app's stylesheets and importmap from `origin`, which the
document declares in the resource's CSP lists, so the Rails asset
pipeline and Poetry's controllers run inside the sandbox as they
are. `assets: :inline` writes the compiled stylesheets into the
document and leaves the page without a JavaScript runtime beyond
the bridge: the fallback for a host that loads nothing external.

bridge fills its regions from the fragments each tool result
carries.

objects.docstring:
The host side of MCP Apps: other servers' apps inside a Rails page.
A host knows its servers (an id, a URL, the headers it holds for
them), reads their tools and app resources through its own client
(cached), calls tools for the page, answers an app's own requests
through an allowlist and the tool visibility the server declared,

origin by default, with the resource's policy as a header.

it mounts the frame an app renders in, speaks the bridge, and sends
the app's requests to {RpcApp} (or a controller of the application's
own that calls {#rpc} with the signed-in user's headers).

objects.docstring:
The Rails engine: merges the WebMCP controllers manifest into
poetry-core's catalog (so `webmcp:` roots validate at render), serves
the runtime JavaScript through the importmap-first channel, and
mounts the origin-trial middleware. Loading the gem is the only
integration step; the host imports `@poetry/agent` beside
`@poetry/controllers`.

The MCP server projecting the component contract
over Model Context Protocol so an agent in Claude Code / Cursor queries
the LIVE registry and runs the linter as a tool. Thin - it projects the
surfaces already built (Registry + LlmsText + Check), never a second
source. Read-only, progressive-disclosure (brief|detailed|full), and
verdict-returning (check returns per-finding pass/fail).

Two transports, one server, on the official `mcp` gem: the gem speaks
JSON-RPC 2.0, negotiates the protocol version, validates a call's
arguments against the tool's schema and serves Streamable HTTP; this
class owns the roster and the tools. Newline-delimited JSON-RPC over
stdio is the `poetry-agent` exe ({Server#serve}); POST JSON-RPC over
HTTP is {HTTP}, for the same-origin `/mcp` mount in-page bridges read.
{Server#handle} is a pure request->response function (testable without
either transport); {Bundled} is the one assembly both transports share;
{Server#mcp} is the gem's server, open to a host's own tools.

v1 is the read/verify surface. The heavier roadmap - verify_screen
running the eval gate array, component:// artifact resources, tag
browsing, SSE streaming - is maturity-gated and NOT in this cut.

objects.docstring:
Per-user authorization for the HTTP mount, the resource-server half
of MCP's authorization specification on the gem's own stack: the
protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) a host reads to find the
authorization server, the bearer challenge a request without a
token gets, and the verification of the token every request
carries. Poetry never issues tokens: the application (Doorkeeper,
say) or an identity provider is the authorization server, and the
verifier is how this server recognizes that server's tokens.

A verified token is the request's identity: handlers built on the
gem read it as `server_context.auth_info`, and anything rendering
for the request (a document, a fragment, a tool) reads {.current}.

auth = Poetry::Agent::MCP::Auth.new(
  resource: "https://shop.example/mcp", authorization_servers: ["https://shop.example"],
  scopes: ["mcp"],
  verifier: ->(token) do
    record = Doorkeeper::AccessToken.by_token(token)
    { subject: record.resource_owner_id.to_s, scopes: record.scopes.to_a,
      expires_at: record.expires_at&.to_i } if record&.accessible?
  end
)
mount auth.metadata_app => auth.well_known_path
mount Poetry::Agent::MCP::HTTP.new(server, auth: auth) => "/mcp"

objects.docstring:
The MCP server over HTTP: the gem's Streamable HTTP transport, as a
Rack app, in its stateless JSON mode (one POST, one JSON reply; no
session to keep, no event stream to hold), over the same server the
stdio exe serves - one surface, two transports. Mount it at the
conventional same-origin `/mcp`, which is where in-page bridges
(WebMCP site MCP server packs among them) look for a site's own MCP
server; a browser client sends `Accept: application/json`.

Read-only by construction (every tool describes or verifies), so
exposing it is a discovery surface, not a mutation surface. The
Origin header is validated against the request's own host, so a
cross-site page cannot drive it through a visitor's browser;
`allowed_origins:` names the other origins to let in. The Host
header is the host application's to validate (Rails does), so the
transport's own loopback-only host check stays off.

With `auth:` (an {Auth}) the mount is a protected resource: every
request needs a bearer token the application's verifier knows, a
request without one is challenged with the metadata's address, and
the verified token is the request's identity ({Auth.current}).

The WebMCP runtime's Ruby side. The contract itself lives in
poetry-core (the `tool` declarations, their registry projection, and
the per-instance `webmcp:` payload a component root carries); this
module owns what only the runtime gem knows: the Stimulus controller
identifiers the JS registers, the controllers manifest that lets
core's attribute builder validate them, and origin-trial delivery.

Nothing here exposes a tool by itself - a rendered instance opts in
(`webmcp: "country"` on the helper call), and the registrar
controller registers that instance's declared tools with
`document.modelContext` on connect, aborting them on disconnect.
